title.zh: 沒人看見就沒關係？跨90國研究揭開日常行為背後的「觀眾效應」與階級壓力
title.en: Does It Matter If Anyone's Watching? A 90-Society Study of How Observers and Status Shape Everyday Norms

summary.zh:
【總結】這項發表於《美國社會學評論》的跨國研究，基於25,000多名參與者、90個社會的數據，首次系統性地證實了日常行為的規範約束具有「關係性條件」：當有他人在場時，人們會顯著收斂行為；而當觀察者地位更高時，約束更強。研究同時發現，這種「觀眾效應」在強調個人化道德（避免傷害他人、追求公平）的社會中更為強烈，而「地位效應」則幾乎跨文化普遍存在。這項研究打通了社會規範理論、地位階層與跨文化道德心理學，為理解日常社會秩序如何維持提供了堅實的實證基礎。

【研究問題】社會學經典理論長期關注規範如何被「內化」——即人們即使無人監督也會遵守規則。然而，當代研究指出規範的本質在於行為對他人產生的外部性，卻鮮少系統性地檢驗「他人在場」本身如何改變人們對日常行為的判斷。過去研究也缺乏跨文化視角來探討觀眾效應與地位效應是否普遍存在，以及文化道德價值如何調節這些效應。解決這一問題至關重要，因為它直接關乎我們如何理解社會秩序的運作機制，以及不平等是如何在日常互動中被複製的。

【研究方法】研究團隊利用「全球日常規範研究」（GSEN）的數據，採用受控實驗設計：每位參與者評估15種日常行為（如爭吵、大笑、罵人、親吻、哭泣、唱歌、講電話、 flirt、戴耳機、看報、討價還價、進食、休息、憤怒大喊、使用手機）在不同觀察者情境下的適當性——包括「獨自一人」「在同事／同學面前」和「在管理層／教授面前」。研究同時測量參與者的個人化 versus 束縛性道德基礎（IM），並控制人類發展指數、宗教程度、年齡、性別等變項，採用多層混合效應模型進行分析。

【結果】研究發現，15種行為中，除了講電話外，其餘14種在「有同儕在場」時都被認為較不適當，觀眾效應在90個社會中幾乎普遍存在。地位效應同樣顯著：在所有15種行為上，「在高地位者面前」的適當性評分都低於「在同儕面前」。更具意義的是文化差異：在個人化道德較高的社會（如瑞典、芬蘭、捷克），觀眾效應更強——這些社會在無人時對行為最為寬容，但一旦有人便在場就明顯收斂；而在束縛性道德較高的社會（如衣索比亞、沙烏地阿拉伯），無論是否有人，行為約束都相對一致。地位效應在個體層面也受IM調節，但在社會層面則無顯著關聯，暗示個體價值與文化脈絡可能存在相互抵消的機制。
summary.en:
**Summary:** Published in the American Sociological Review, this cross-national study draws on data from over 25,000 participants across 90 societies to provide the first systematic evidence that norms governing everyday behaviors are relationally contingent: the mere presence of others significantly constrains behavior, and this constraint intensifies further when observers hold higher status. The research also reveals that the observer effect is stronger in societies prioritizing individualizing morality (avoiding harm and unfairness), while the status effect is nearly universal across cultures. By bridging social norm theory, status hierarchy research, and cross-cultural moral psychology, the study offers a robust empirical foundation for understanding how everyday social order is maintained and how inequality is reproduced through routine interaction.

**Problem:** Classical sociological theories of norms have long emphasized internalization—the idea that people follow rules even when unobserved because they have absorbed social expectations. Yet contemporary approaches argue that norms exist precisely because behaviors impose costs or benefits on others, making the presence of observers central. Despite this theoretical insight, no study has systematically tested how the mere presence of others shapes normative judgments across a wide range of everyday behaviors, nor has prior research examined whether observer and status effects vary across cultures or how moral foundations moderate these effects. Addressing this gap is crucial because it goes to the heart of how social order works and how hierarchies are reproduced in daily life.

**Approach:** The researchers used data from the Global Study of Everyday Norms (GSEN), employing a controlled experimental design. Each participant rated the appropriateness of 15 everyday behaviors—including arguing, laughing, cursing, kissing, crying, singing, talking on the phone, flirting, listening to headphones, reading a newspaper, bargaining, eating, resting, shouting in anger, and using a mobile phone—across three observer contexts: alone, in front of peers, and in front of higher-status others (e.g., management or professors). The study also measured participants' individualizing versus binding moral foundations (IM) and controlled for HDI, religiosity, age, and gender. Multilevel mixed-effects models were used to account for the nested structure of the data.

**Results:** The findings show that for 14 of the 15 behaviors (talking being the exception), appropriateness ratings dropped significantly when peers were present compared to being alone, with observer effects ranging from -0.56 (bargaining) to -2.15 (kissing) on the appropriateness scale. The status effect was equally consistent: all 15 behaviors were rated as more inappropriate in front of higher-status observers than in front of peers. Culturally, the observer effect was notably larger in societies scoring higher on individualizing morality (e.g., Sweden, Finland, Czech Republic)—these societies were especially permissive when alone but became markedly more constrained in public. In contrast, binding-morality societies (e.g., Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia, Benin) showed relatively consistent constraints regardless of observers. At the individual level, higher IM predicted stronger status effects, but at the societal level no such relationship was found, suggesting compositional and contextual forces may offset each other.

keyArticle.title: How Norms Depend on the Presence and Status of Observers: The Relational Contingency of Everyday Behaviors in 90 Societies
